An idolater is a person who worships an idol — or, more broadly, someone who is devoted to something or someone with an extreme, almost god-like level of reverence.

To truly understand "idolater," you first need to understand what an idol is.

An idol is a physical object — a statue, a figurine, a carved image, a painting — that a person or group of people treats as a god, or as a direct stand-in for a god. Instead of worshipping an invisible, abstract divine being, they direct their worship at this physical object. They may bow before it, offer it gifts, pray to it, believe it has divine power, or consider it sacred and holy.

An idolater, then, is the person doing this. It is someone who worships such an object as if it were a god.

The word is most at home in a religious context, and this is its original, most precise meaning.

In the world's major monotheistic religions — Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — idolatry is considered one of the gravest sins possible. The core belief in these faiths is that there is only one God, and that God is not a physical object. Therefore, anyone who directs worship toward a statue or image is committing a serious spiritual error. That person is called an idolater.

For example, in the Bible, when the ancient Israelites melted their gold jewelry and shaped it into a golden calf and began to worship it — they were acting as idolaters. The calf was their idol.

Similarly, in ancient civilisations like Greece, Rome, Egypt, or Mesopotamia, people worshipped many gods, and those gods were often represented by statues in temples. From the strict perspective of a monotheistic believer, those worshippers were idolaters.

So in its sharpest religious sense, an idolater is:

A person who worships a physical image or object as a god (or in place of God).

The practice itself is called idolatry, and the adjective form is idolatrous (meaning "relating to or characteristic of an idolater").
The Negative Weight of the Word

It is important to understand that "idolater" is almost never a neutral word. It almost always carries a critical or disapproving tone. It implies:

  • That the person is worshipping something that is not truly worthy of worship.
  • That their devotion is misplaced, blind, or misguided.
  • That they are, in some sense, being foolish — pouring reverence into something that cannot receive or return it in any meaningful way.

When someone calls another person an idolater, they are not simply describing a behaviour — they are usually judging it.

In modern everyday English, the word has stretched beyond its strict religious meaning. People now use "idolater" more loosely to describe anyone who admires or adores a person, a celebrity, an ideology, or even a material object with excessive, uncritical, almost worshipful devotion — as if that thing were a god.

For example:

  • "He is a complete idolater of that football player — he has posters of him everywhere, defends everything he does, and cannot hear a single word of criticism about him."
  • "She's an idolater of money — she has made it the central purpose of her entire existence."

In these cases, no literal statue or temple is involved. But the quality of the devotion is what earns the label: it is blind, total, and uncritical — the same qualities that define religious idol worship.

This figurative use is also critical in tone. Calling someone an idolater is a way of saying: "You have elevated something to a status it does not deserve, and it has taken over your better judgement."
The Key Qualities That Define an Idolater

Whether used literally or figuratively, the word "idolater" almost always implies the following qualities in the person being described:

  1. Excessive devotion — Their admiration goes far beyond what is reasonable or proportionate.
  2. Blind loyalty — They do not question or critically examine the object of their worship.
  3. Misplaced reverence — They are directing their devotion at something that does not truly deserve that level of worship.
  4. Total surrender — The idol (or idol-equivalent) has become the central, organising force of their life.

• "The ancient city was full of idolaters who brought offerings to stone statues every morning."
  • "The preacher warned his congregation not to become idolaters by placing wealth above God."
  • "Critics accused the fans of being idolaters — they celebrated their favourite singer's every move regardless of what he did."
An idolater is a person who worships a physical idol as a god — and, more broadly, anyone who gives a person, object, or idea a level of blind, excessive, uncritical devotion that borders on worship.
